result: Repeated blood sampling after exercise and after total sleep deprivation showed no clinically significant upregulation of proinflammatory cytokines in CFS (plasma protein, PBL mRNA, resting and stimulated PBL function).
reason: Tests stimulated immune-cell cytokine responses after exertion and finds no exaggeration; stimulant not specified as microbial and abstract gives no numbers.

result: Post-exercise PBL cytokine mRNA (and plasma protein) did not rise meaningfully in CFS versus controls.
reason: Post-exercise leukocyte mRNA for immune genes is part of the claim; null result, though it does not test the sensory/adrenergic receptor genes.

result: Meta-analysis of case-control CFS studies found an attenuated cortisol awakening increase (d=-0.34) but no significant difference in CAR output or circadian cortisol output.
reason: Same salivary awakening/diurnal cortisol output measures, no group difference; earlier and smaller than Woo 2026.

result: Systematic review of 6 CFS case-control studies found HRV reduced only during sleep, with increased sympathetic activity only at night.
reason: Daytime resting HRV not reduced contradicts the resting claim; small review superseded by Nelson 2019; the nocturnal result also fits neuro-nocturnal-hrv.

result: In 343 Fukuda CFS patients with one-night PSG, 30.3% had a primary sleep disorder; among the other 239, 89.1% had at least one objective sleep problem and four phenotypes emerged (long SOL/REM latency, frequent arousals, long TST, short TST with high WASO).
reason: No control group, so not a replication; adds sleep phenotypes and a high primary sleep disorder rate, which tempers the 'no clinical disorder' part of the claim.

result: In 33 CFS vs 24 controls, naive B cells were higher (65% vs 47% of B cells, p=0.003), transitional B cells higher (1.8% vs 0.8%) and plasmablasts lower (0.5% vs 0.9%).
reason: Independent cohort, same flow-cytometry B-cell subset measure, same direction for naive B cells; does not report switched memory.

result: In 50 CFS vs 50 controls who all passed effort tests, only information processing speed (reaction time) was impaired; attention, memory, motor, verbal and visuospatial performance were comparable, and slowing was unrelated to depression, anxiety, fatigue or sleep.
reason: Replicates the speed deficit but not attention or memory; adds effort-validated testing and independence from mood and fatigue.

result: Five years after Bergen giardiasis, 22 of 53 clinically examined patients with chronic fatigue at 3 years had Fukuda CFS (41.5%), 13.2% idiopathic chronic fatigue, 24.5% fatigue from other causes (sleep apnoea, depression, anxiety), and 20.8% had resolved; fatigue scores fell from year 3 to 5.
reason: Same outbreak cohort, not an independent replication; adds clinical CFS diagnosis, differential diagnoses and natural course (only 53 of 253 invited took part).

result: Of 179 CDC-1994 CFS clinic patients, 13% (n=24) had POTS; they were younger (29 vs 42 years) and had distinct autonomic and clinical features that symptom scales could pick out.
reason: The prevalence falls within the 6-43% range and the paper adds a clinical profile of the POTS subgroup.

result: Of 179 CFS patients, 13% had POTS and were a younger, clinically distinct subgroup.
reason: Does not measure cerebral blood flow or preload, the core of this finding; the prevalence data are already covered by the neuro-pots-prevalence link.
